v.q: You build `list.stream().filter(p).map(f)` and never call a terminal operation. What happens?
o: Nothing runs: intermediate operations are lazy
The pipeline runs and results are discarded
The pipeline runs and the list is modified
It does not compile without a terminal call
v.w: Streams are lazy. Only a terminal operation such as `collect`, `count` or `forEach` triggers the work.

v.q: When does the code in filter and map actually run?
o: When a terminal operation is called
When the stream is created
When the filter is declared
When the list is sorted
v.w: Intermediate operations are lazy. The terminal operation pulls elements through the pipeline.

v.q: What happens if you call a terminal operation twice on the same stream?
o: `IllegalStateException`: the stream was already operated upon
The second call returns the same result again
The second call returns an empty result
The stream restarts from the first element
v.w: Streams are single-use. Call `stream()` on the source again for another pass.

v.q: Which statement about reusing a stream is NOT true?
o: A stream can be consumed again after collect
A second terminal call throws IllegalStateException
You can create a new stream from the same source
A stream is a one-shot pipeline
v.w: A stream can only be consumed once. Create a new one from the source.

v.q: A stream of customers, each with a list of accounts. Which operation yields one flat `Stream<Account>`?
o: `flatMap(c -> c.accounts().stream())`
`map(Customer::accounts)`
`filter(c -> !c.accounts().isEmpty())`
`collect(Collectors.toList())`
v.w: `map` gives a `Stream<List<Account>>`. `flatMap` flattens the inner streams into one.

v.q: Which operation turns Stream<List<Account>> into Stream<Account>?
o: flatMap
map
filter
peek
v.w: flatMap replaces each element with a stream and joins them. map would keep the lists nested.

v.q: `Collectors.toMap(Account::branch, Account::id)` is used on accounts where two share a branch. What happens?
o: `IllegalStateException` for the duplicate key
The second value silently replaces the first
Both values are stored in a list
The duplicate is skipped and the stream continues
v.w: `toMap` fails on duplicates unless you give a merge function, or use `groupingBy` to collect all values per key.

v.q: Which toMap overload handles duplicate keys without an exception?
o: The one with a merge function
The two-argument version
The one that takes only a key mapper
Collectors.counting()
v.w: A merge function decides what to do with two values for the same key, for example keeping the larger.

v.q: Which collector splits accounts into exactly two groups, active and inactive?
o: `partitioningBy(Account::isActive)`
`groupingBy(Account::branch)`
`toMap(Account::id, Account::isActive)`
`counting()`
v.w: `partitioningBy` always returns a map with both a `true` and a `false` key. `groupingBy` can have any number of keys.

v.q: Which collector builds a Map<String, List<Account>> by branch?
o: groupingBy
partitioningBy
joining
summingInt
v.w: groupingBy returns a map from the key to a list. partitioningBy has only true and false groups.

v.q: Which parallel stream use is the most likely to be correct and fast?
o: A pure CPU-heavy computation over a large `ArrayList`
Calling a remote service for each element
Adding results to a shared `ArrayList` from the lambda
Streaming a tiny list of five elements
v.w: Parallel streams use the shared common pool and need stateless, CPU-bound work on large, splittable data. Always measure.

v.q: Which parallel stream use is NOT sensible?
o: Adding results to a shared ArrayList
A pure computation over a large ArrayList
Summing numbers in a big array
A CPU-bound transformation
v.w: A shared mutable list is not thread-safe. Collect results with collect() instead.

v.q: What is the difference between `reduce` and `collect`?
o: `collect` is a mutable reduction into a container, `reduce` folds into one value
`reduce` builds lists and maps, `collect` only adds numbers
`reduce` is lazy and `collect` is eager
They are the same operation with different names
v.w: Building a list with `reduce` copies it at every step. `collect` is designed for containers and is parallel-safe.

v.q: Which call computes the sum of ints as a reduction to one value?
o: reduce(0, Integer::sum)
collect(Collectors.toList())
peek(System.out::println)
sorted()
v.w: reduce folds elements into a single value. collect builds a container.

v.q: Why is `peek` a poor place for required logic?
o: It may not run at all, for example after short-circuiting or when the size is known
It always runs twice for each element
It modifies the elements of the source
It forces the stream to become parallel
v.w: `peek` exists mainly for debugging. Required side effects belong in a terminal operation such as `forEach`.

v.q: Which statement about peek is NOT true?
o: It is guaranteed to run for every element
It is meant for debugging
It may be skipped by optimisation
Required logic does not belong in it
v.w: The stream may skip it, for example after short-circuiting or when the count is known.
